title: Universes of the past and future
one_line_summary: A guided tour of a numbered zoo of Friedmann model universes (Universes 2 to 11): flat radiation, dust and dust-plus-Lambda models, closed and open dust models, and the k = 1 family built around Einstein's static universe (its instability, Lemaitre's coasting model, the Eddington-Lemaitre and bouncing models), closed by the historical route from Einstein's 1917 static model through Hubble, the time-scale problem, the Lambda = 0 'standard models' and the CMB.
role_in_book: Payoff chapter of Part III. Chapter 15 introduced the cosmological principle and Universes 0 and 1, Chapter 16 built the three Robertson-Walker geometries, and Chapter 17 derived the Friedmann equations and the a^-3 and a^-4 dilution laws. Here those tools are exercised: matter content (radiation, dust, vacuum energy of either sign) and spatial curvature k are varied one at a time and the resulting a(t) is solved exactly or qualitatively, producing a catalogue summarized in a single grid figure. The chapter deliberately stays with Big-Bang singularities, horizons and de Sitter geometry at a descriptive level; Chapter 19 takes up Penrose diagrams, the de Sitter spacetime proper and the nature of the initial singularity, the exercises preview de Sitter space as a hyperboloid, and the present-day observational verdict (dark energy, flatness) is deferred to Section 49.8. The Lambda = 0 'standard models' and 'missing mass' discussion reflect the pre-1998 picture and must be updated by the tutor.

assumed_background.topic: Robertson-Walker line element for k = 0, +1, -1 and the meaning of the scale factor a(t)
First and second Friedmann equations with a cosmological constant, in G = c = 1 units
Dilution laws rho_dust proportional to a^-3 and rho_radiation proportional to a^-4 from the first law of thermodynamics
Universe 0 (empty, flat) and Universe 1 (flat de Sitter expansion driven by Lambda)
Hubble parameter, Hubble flow and proper distance growth
Critical density and its link to spatial flatness
Vacuum energy as a fluid with negative pressure p = -rho
Separable first-order ODEs, substitution and standard integrals (arcsin, arsinh), hyperbolic functions
Taylor expansion about an equilibrium and linear stability (exponential vs oscillatory solutions)
Energy-equation / effective-potential method for one-dimensional motion
Minkowski line elements and coordinate transformations such as Rindler-type hyperbolic coordinates
Embedding a surface in a higher-dimensional flat space to read off an induced metric
Galaxy recession, Hubble's law, megaparsec units and black-body radiation temperature

learning_objectives: Reader can derive a(t) for flat radiation-filled (a proportional to t^1/2) and flat dust-filled (a proportional to t^2/3) universes from the first Friedmann equation and state H(t) = 1/(2t) and 2/(3t) respectively.
Reader can explain why a density that scales as a negative power of a forces a(0) = 0 and an infinite initial density, i.e. a Big-Bang singularity, while pure de Sitter expansion has none.

Reader can write the combined dust-plus-vacuum first Friedmann equation adot^2 + k = C/a + (Lambda/3) a^2 and use term dominance at small and large a to predict late and early behaviour before solving.
Reader can show that a negative cosmological constant stops expansion at a^3 = 3C/(-Lambda) and leads to a Big Crunch even in a flat universe.
Reader can integrate the closed (k = 1) and open (k = -1) Lambda = 0 dust models by the substitution u^2 = a/C and describe their fates (recollapse vs unbounded growth).
Reader can derive the Einstein static universe conditions k = 1, a0 = Lambda_E^-1/2, rho = Lambda_E/(4 pi) and prove it is unstable by linearizing the acceleration equation with mass conservation.

Reader can recast the k = 1 dust-plus-Lambda equation as adot^2 + 1 = V_eff(a) and use the shape of V_eff to explain the Lemaitre coasting phase, the Eddington-Lemaitre model, and the bouncing Universe 11.
Reader can estimate the coasting duration of a Lemaitre universe and explain why it grows only logarithmically as Lambda approaches Lambda_E.
Reader can read the (k, Lambda) grid of a(t) curves and predict the origin (Big Bang or not) and fate (crunch, unbounded expansion, asymptotic static) of a model from its position.
Reader can use the tangent-line construction to show that a monotonically decelerating universe is younger than 1/H_now, and explain how the time-scale problem arose and was resolved.

Reader can outline the historical sequence (Einstein 1917, de Sitter 1917, Friedmann 1922, Lemaitre 1927/1931, Hubble 1929, Eddington 1930, Robertson-Walker 1935, Alpher-Herman 1948, Penzias-Wilson 1964) and say which numbered universe each proposal corresponds to.
Reader can compute the critical density in SI units from H0 = 100h km/s/Mpc and compare it with the observed density of luminous matter.

Reader can (via the exercises) represent de Sitter spacetime as a hyperboloid in a higher-dimensional Minkowski space and recognize that different slicings give flat, closed, open or static line elements.

teaching_approach.summary: A catalogue chapter organized as a controlled experiment: the Friedmann machinery from Chapter 17 is held fixed while the ingredients (radiation, dust, positive or negative vacuum energy) and the curvature constant k are changed one at a time, each resulting model receiving a number and a stacked-slice cartoon of its history. Exact solutions are shown when they are compact, but the authors lean repeatedly on 'which term dominates at small or large a' reasoning, then consolidate in a comparison table and a 5-by-3 grid of a(t) sketches. The k = 1 family is organized around Einstein's static universe, analysed with a linear perturbation; the Lemaitre model is then treated with an effective potential V_eff(a) whose shallow minimum (a point of slowest expansion) produces the coasting phase, while the Eddington-Lemaitre and 0 < Lambda < Lambda_E models are described only qualitatively through initial conditions and sketched radius functions. Only after the logical tour do the authors tell the historical story, deliberately contrasting logical order with discovery order, and use a tangent-line age argument to explain why Lambda was once needed and then abandoned.
narrative_arc: Recall the RW metric, both Friedmann equations and H = adot/a in a margin box; announce a survey of numbered universes classified by k, starting from a known a(t0).

Flat models: recall empty Universe 0 and de Sitter Universe 1 (no Big Bang); insert radiation (Universe 2, a proportional to t^1/2) and dust (Universe 3, Einstein-de Sitter, a proportional to t^2/3), showing both begin at a = 0 with infinite density; tabulate the three.

Mix dust and positive Lambda (Universe 4): predict t^2/3 early and exponential late by term dominance, then quote the exact cosh solution; flip the sign of Lambda (Universe 5) to get turnaround and a Big Crunch.
Curve space with Lambda = 0 (Universes 6 and 7): integrate the closed case in a worked example by substitution, quote the open case, and summarize that only k = 1 recollapses.
Seek a static solution (Universe 8): both Friedmann equations force k = 1 and a tuned dust density; perturb it and find exponential runaway, so the balance is unstable.
Push Lambda slightly above Lambda_E (Universe 9): introduce an effective potential, locate the minimum of adot, expand about it and show the coasting time scales as ln(1/epsilon).

Complete the k = 1 family: Eddington-Lemaitre (Universe 10, leaving or approaching the static state) and 0 < Lambda < Lambda_E (Universe 11, recollapse or bounce); gather everything in the (k, Lambda) grid of Fig. 18.10.

Re-tell the story in historical order: static Einstein model, de Sitter, Friedmann, Lemaitre, Hubble's law, instability, dropping Lambda, Primeval Atom and Hoyle's 'Big Bang' label, Robertson-Walker generality.

Pose the time-scale problem with a tangent-line bound on the age (Example 18.7), then show how revised H0 values in the 1950s removed the need for Lambda, making the Lambda = 0 Big-Bang models 'standard'.

Close with hot Big Bang nucleosynthesis, CMB prediction and discovery, critical density numbers and the missing mass puzzle, and hand off to the Big-Bang singularity in the next chapter; exercises build de Sitter space as a hyperboloid.
signature_moves: Numbering every model (Universe 0 to 11) so that later text, figures and the summary grid can refer to them as named characters.
Stacked-slice cartoons that encode both spatial geometry (square grids for flat, circles for 3-spheres, funnel sections for hyperbolic space) and the size history a(t) in one 3D sketch.
Predicting asymptotic behaviour from which term of the Friedmann equation dominates at small or large a before quoting an exact solution.

Treating the k = 1 dust-plus-Lambda equation like a particle energy equation, adot^2 + 1 = V_eff(a), so that coasting is explained by V_eff barely exceeding 1 near its minimum (the book uses this device for Universe 9 only; extending it to Universes 8, 10 and 11 is a natural tutor move).
Linear perturbation of an equilibrium using the conservation law rho a^3 = const to close the equation, borrowed from a problem-book approach.
A one-page grid (k columns, Lambda rows) that turns the whole chapter into a lookup table of origins and fates.

Presenting physics in logical order first and history afterwards, with an explicit remark that the two orders differ, then using an elementary geometric construction (tangent line) to make a historical controversy quantitative.
Exercises that preview advanced geometry (de Sitter hyperboloid, slicings, Poincaré patch, static patch) in a 2D toy version.

sections.title: Chapter opening: the toolkit recalled
sections.summary: After a Darwin epigraph about the struggle for existence, the authors restate the Robertson-Walker line element and, in a shaded margin box, both Friedmann equations and the Hubble parameter with its role in proper-distance growth. Universes will be stocked with perfect fluid plus vacuum energy, sorted by k, and each evolved from a known value of a at some reference time t0; Universes 0 and 1 from earlier chapters are flagged as the flat starting point.
key_moves: Treat a(t) as an effective radius of the universe.
Classify models first by k, then by matter content.
Fix initial data by specifying a(t0).

sections.title: Spatially flat universes
sections.summary: Flat models are built one ingredient at a time. Universe 0 is empty Minkowski space; Universe 1 (de Sitter) expands exponentially with constant H = sqrt(Lambda/3) and has no singularity. Radiation (Universe 2) gives a proportional to t^1/2 and dust (Universe 3, Einstein-de Sitter) gives a proportional to t^2/3; both start at zero size with infinite density and have H decaying as 1/(2t) and 2/(3t) (Example 18.1). A table compares the three flat models. Adding positive Lambda to dust (Universe 4) interpolates from t^2/3 to exponential growth with an exact cosh^(1/3) solution; a negative Lambda (Universe 5) instead halts expansion at a^3 = 3C/(-Lambda) and recollapses to a Big Crunch, with an exact (1 - cos)^(1/3) solution. A footnote introduces the general dust-plus-Lambda equation (18.11) used for the rest of the chapter.
concepts: flat dust plus cosmological constant universe
key_moves: Substitute rho proportional to a^-4 or a^-3 into the k = Lambda = 0 Friedmann equation and separate variables.
Differentiate a(t) to show H = 1/(2t), so H0 = 1/(2t0) and rho diverges at t = 0.
Collect composition, a(t), H(t) and presence of a Big Bang into a comparison table.
Argue from term dominance that dust controls early times and Lambda controls late times, then quote the exact solution.
Note that negative vacuum energy acts like attractive positive-pressure matter, find the zero of the right-hand side, and quote the recollapsing exact solution.

sections.title: Curved universes with Lambda = 0
sections.summary: With Lambda = 0 the dust Friedmann equation becomes adot^2 + k = C/a. Example 18.2 solves the closed case (Universe 6) by the substitution u^2 = a/C and Big-Bang initial conditions, giving t(a) in closed form (arcsin minus a square-root term): the model rises from zero, reaches a maximum and collapses. The open case (Universe 7) is obtained analogously with arsinh and grows without bound, faster than Einstein-de Sitter. Stacked cartoons show 3-spheres for k = 1 and hyperbolic slices for k = -1, and a three-panel plot compares the k = 1, 0, -1 radius functions.
key_moves: Change variable u^2 = a/C to reduce the closed-dust equation to a standard integral.
Impose a = 0 at t = 0 as the integration constant.
Invert the logic: obtain t(a) rather than a(t) and read the shape from the graph.
Replace trigonometric by hyperbolic functions for k = -1.
Conclude that with Lambda = 0 geometry decides fate: only k = 1 recollapses.

sections.title: Einstein, Lemaître and Eddington
sections.summary: Seeking a time-independent model, Example 18.3 sets adot = addot = 0 in both Friedmann equations for dust plus Lambda_E and finds that k must be +1, with a0 = Lambda_E^-1/2 and rho = Lambda_E/(4 pi): the Einstein static universe (Universe 8). Example 18.4 perturbs a and rho, uses rho a^3 = const, and finds delta a grows like exp(sqrt(Lambda_E) t), so the balance between vacuum push and matter pull is unstable. Universe 9 (Lemaitre) with Lambda slightly above Lambda_E has a coasting period: writing adot^2 + 1 = V_eff(a) (Example 18.5), the expansion rate is smallest at a_min = (1+epsilon)^(1/3)/sqrt(Lambda), and expanding V_eff about that point (Example 18.6) gives a sinh solution whose plateau lasts a time of order ln(1/epsilon)/sqrt(Lambda) before de Sitter-like growth resumes. Universe 10 (Eddington-Lemaitre) either leaves the static state or approaches it asymptotically from a Big Bang; Universe 11 (0 < Lambda < Lambda_E) either recollapses from a Big Bang or bounces from exponential contraction to exponential expansion. Fig. 18.10 gathers representative a(t) curves on a k-versus-Lambda grid.
concepts: instability of the Einstein static universe
effective potential for the scale factor
key_moves: Use the second Friedmann equation at rest to get k/a0^2 = Lambda_E, which forces k = +1.
Subtract the Friedmann equations to isolate addot, perturb about equilibrium, and close with delta rho/rho = -3 delta a/a.
Rescale dust density in Einstein-universe units and write Lambda = (1+epsilon)^2 Lambda_E.
Recast the first Friedmann equation as an energy equation with V_eff(a); locate the minimum of V_eff.
Quadratic expansion of V_eff about its minimum yields a sinh solution; the prefactor sets a logarithmic coasting time.

Describe the remaining k = 1 cases (Eddington-Lemaitre and 0 < Lambda < Lambda_E) qualitatively, distinguishing branches by initial conditions and pointing to the sketched radius functions of Fig. 18.9(b,c) and the grid of Fig. 18.10.

sections.title: A brief history of model universes
sections.summary: The models are re-ordered historically: Einstein's 1917 static closed universe with a cosmological term, de Sitter's Lambda-only model, Friedmann's evolving solutions (1922), Weyl's remark on test-particle recession (1923), Lemaitre's independent derivation and expanding model (1927) championed by Eddington, Hubble's distance-velocity law (1929), Eddington's instability proof (1930), Einstein abandoning Lambda (1931), Lemaitre's Primeval Atom (1931), and Robertson and Walker's generality proof (1935). Example 18.7 uses a tangent to a(t) to show a decelerating universe is younger than 1/H_now; with pre-1950 values (about 1.8 billion years) this clashed with uranium-dated rocks at least 3 billion years old, the time-scale problem. Large Lambda or the Eddington-Lemaitre model offered escapes, but 1950s revisions of H0 lengthened the age to about 13 billion years, restoring Lambda = 0 Big-Bang 'standard models' (Universes 3, 6, 7). Nucleosynthesis in a hot early universe, the 1948 Alpher-Herman CMB prediction (about 5 K) and the 1964 Penzias-Wilson discovery (2.73 K) supported the Big Bang. The critical density 1.88e-26 h^2 kg/m^3 is compared with a luminous matter density near 1e-28 kg/m^3 despite evidence for flatness, labelled the missing mass problem.
concepts: Hubble time as an age bound
key_moves: Explicitly contrast the logical order of the models with the order in which they were proposed.
Draw the tangent to a(t) at t_now and show its intercept lies earlier than the true origin for a decelerating curve.
Compare the Hubble-time bound with radiometric Earth ages to expose a contradiction.
Show how revised measurements (timeline plot of H0) removed the contradiction and the motivation for Lambda.
Use T proportional to 1/a to connect the Big Bang to element synthesis and a relic radiation field.
Express rho_c numerically via h and compare with observed matter density.

sections.title: Chapter summary and exercises: Milne and de Sitter geometry
sections.summary: The summary recaps that perfect-fluid RW models mostly start with a Big Bang, that Einstein's static model is unstable while Einstein-de Sitter expands forever and Lemaitre's model coasts, and that the Lambda = 0 standard models all have an initial singularity. The eight exercises cover the empty k = -1 model (Milne universe) as flat spacetime in disguise, substitution checks of the Universe 4 and 5 solutions and of the stability and coasting algebra, and a sequence on de Sitter spacetime embedded as a hyperboloid in 4+1 (and toy 2+1 and 1+1) Minkowski space, where different coordinate choices give closed, open, flat-expanding, Poincaré and static line elements covering different portions of the hyperboloid.
concepts: coordinate slicings of de Sitter spacetime
key_moves: Show the empty open universe is Minkowski space via r = t sinh chi, T = t cosh chi.
Embed hyperbola and hyperboloid in flat Lorentzian space and read off induced metrics.
Recognize that the same spacetime admits slicings with different spatial curvature, so k is a property of the slicing, not only of the spacetime.
Identify coordinate patches that cover only part of the hyperboloid.

concepts.name: Robertson-Walker metric
concepts.definition: The most general spacetime metric compatible with spatial homogeneity and isotropy: ds^2 = -dt^2 + a(t)^2 [dr^2/(1-kr^2) + r^2 dOmega^2], with a single time-dependent scale factor and constant spatial curvature sign k.
concepts.how_introduced: Restated at the chapter start as the common geometric backdrop of every model; in the history section the authors note Robertson and Walker proved its generality in 1935.

concepts.name: Friedmann equations
concepts.definition: The time-time and space-space components of Einstein's equation for a Robertson-Walker metric filled with perfect fluid and vacuum energy: (adot/a)^2 + k/a^2 = 8 pi rho/3 + Lambda/3 and 2 addot/a + (adot/a)^2 + k/a^2 = -8 pi p + Lambda (G = c = 1).
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled in a margin box; the first equation drives almost every model, and the second is used to impose staticity and to derive the acceleration equation for the stability analysis.

concepts.name: dust-plus-vacuum Friedmann equation
aliases: master equation for dust and Lambda
concepts.definition: For a universe containing only pressureless matter and a cosmological constant, the first Friedmann equation multiplied by a^2 becomes adot^2 + k = C/a + (Lambda/3) a^2 with C = (8 pi/3) rho_d a^3, a constant fixed by the conserved amount of dust.
concepts.how_introduced: Slipped in as a footnote while treating flat dust plus Lambda, then promoted to the working equation for curved models and the basis for computing every panel of the summary grid.
prerequisites: scaling of energy density with the scale factor
concepts.notes: Formally identical to an energy equation for a particle in a potential -C/a - Lambda a^2/3 with total energy -k; the chapter exploits this only for k = 1.

concepts.name: scale factor
concepts.definition: The function a(t) multiplying the spatial part of the Robertson-Walker metric; ratios a(t2)/a(t1) give how much all comoving proper distances have grown, and for k = +1 it is literally the radius of the 3-sphere.
concepts.how_introduced: Called the expansion factor and informally the effective radius; each model is characterized by its 'radius function' plotted against t.
concepts.notes: For k = 0 and k = -1 space is infinite, so 'radius' is only a figure of speech there.

concepts.name: curvature constant k
concepts.definition: The constant in the Robertson-Walker metric taking values +1 (spatial 3-spheres), 0 (flat space) or -1 (hyperbolic space) after rescaling coordinates.
concepts.how_introduced: Used as the primary organizing label: flat universes first, then k = +1 and k = -1, and as the column heading of the summary grid.

concepts.name: Hubble parameter
concepts.definition: H(t) = adot/a, the fractional expansion rate; the proper distance l between comoving observers obeys ldot = H l.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled in the margin; then computed for each flat model to show it is constant only for de Sitter and otherwise decays like 1/t, and finally inverted to bound the age of the universe.

concepts.name: scaling of energy density with the scale factor
concepts.definition: For conserved pressureless matter rho is proportional to a^-3; for radiation the extra redshift of each quantum gives rho proportional to a^-4; vacuum energy density stays constant.
concepts.how_introduced: Taken from the thermodynamic argument of the previous chapter and substituted into the first Friedmann equation to create the radiation and dust models; the dust law rho a^3 = const also closes the stability calculation.

concepts.name: cosmological constant as vacuum energy
concepts.definition: A constant Lambda in Einstein's equation equivalent to a fluid of constant energy density Lambda/(8 pi) and pressure equal to minus that density; positive Lambda accelerates expansion, negative Lambda acts attractively.
concepts.how_introduced: Used as an ingredient that can be switched on with either sign; the text reasons that because positive Lambda carries negative pressure, negative Lambda should behave more like ordinary attracting matter.

concepts.name: empty flat universe
concepts.definition: The Robertson-Walker model with k = 0 and no matter or vacuum energy; it is just Minkowski spacetime.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled from Chapter 15 as the trivial starting member of the catalogue.

concepts.name: de Sitter universe
concepts.definition: The flat Robertson-Walker model containing only positive vacuum energy, expanding as a(t) = a(t0) exp[H(t - t0)] with constant H = sqrt(Lambda/3); it has no Big-Bang singularity.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled from Chapter 15 as the constant-H reference; later it is the late-time attractor of Universes 4 and 9, and the exercises reinterpret it as a slicing of a hyperboloid.

concepts.name: radiation-dominated universe
concepts.definition: The k = Lambda = 0 model filled with radiation (rho proportional to a^-4), for which a(t) = a0 (2 H0 t)^1/2 and H = 1/(2t); it begins at a = 0 with infinite density.
concepts.how_introduced: Built by inserting the radiation dilution law into the flat Friedmann equation, separating variables, and then checking H(t) in Example 18.1.
prerequisites: scaling of energy density with the scale factor

concepts.name: Einstein-de Sitter universe
concepts.definition: The flat, Lambda = 0 universe containing only dust, with a(t) = a0 (3 H0 t/2)^2/3 and H = 2/(3t); it starts from a Big Bang and expands forever with ever-decreasing rate, sitting exactly at the critical density.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived like Universe 2 with rho proportional to a^-3; reused as the small-a limit of dust-plus-Lambda models and as the k = 0 member of the Lambda = 0 'standard models'.
prerequisites: scaling of energy density with the scale factor

concepts.name: Big-Bang singularity
concepts.definition: An initial moment at which the scale factor goes to zero and the energy density (and H) diverge, so the model's spacetime cannot be continued to earlier times.
concepts.how_introduced: Identified in the radiation model from a(0) = 0 and confirmed through H = 1/(2t) growing without limit; later used as a yes/no column in the comparison table and as an initial condition; its physical meaning is postponed to the next chapter.
prerequisites: scaling of energy density with the scale factor

concepts.name: Big-Bang initial conditions
concepts.definition: The choice of integration constant a = 0 at t = 0 when solving the Friedmann equation, which sets the time origin at the singularity so that t measures the age.
concepts.how_introduced: Named in Example 18.2 when integrating the closed dust model.

concepts.name: Big Crunch
concepts.definition: A final singularity in which the scale factor returns to zero after a maximum, the time-reverse of a Big Bang.
concepts.how_introduced: Appears first in the flat negative-Lambda model and then in the closed dust model and one branch of Universe 11.

concepts.name: flat dust plus cosmological constant universe
concepts.definition: The k = 0 model with dust and positive Lambda, a(t) = (3C/2Lambda)^1/3 [cosh(sqrt(3 Lambda) t) - 1]^1/3, which behaves like Einstein-de Sitter at early times and like de Sitter at late times.
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated by asking what happens when vacuum energy is added to Universe 3; the authors first argue from which term wins at small and large a, then quote the exact solution (checked in Exercise 18.2).
concepts.notes: This is structurally the flat Lambda-CDM model of present-day cosmology, though the chapter does not say so.

concepts.name: negative cosmological constant universe
concepts.definition: The k = 0 dust model with Lambda < 0: the right-hand side of adot^2 = C/a + Lambda a^2/3 vanishes at a^3 = 3C/(-Lambda), so expansion halts and the model recollapses, a(t) proportional to [1 - cos(sqrt(-3 Lambda) t)]^1/3.
concepts.how_introduced: Posed as an 'intriguing possibility' and motivated by the sign argument that negative vacuum energy acts like attracting positive-pressure matter.
concepts.notes: The prose calls it vacuum-filled but the solution contains the dust constant C.

concepts.name: closed dust universe
concepts.definition: The k = +1, Lambda = 0 dust model whose spatial slices are 3-spheres; t(a) = C[arcsin sqrt(a/C) - sqrt(a/C) sqrt(1 - a/C)], so a rises from zero to a maximum C and recollapses.
concepts.how_introduced: Worked out fully in Example 18.2 by substitution u^2 = a/C, then pictured as a stack of 3-spheres growing and shrinking.
concepts.notes: Equivalent to the cycloid a = (C/2)(1 - cos eta), t = (C/2)(eta - sin eta), with maximum radius C at t = pi C/2 and crunch at t = pi C (our reformulation).

concepts.name: open dust universe
concepts.definition: The k = -1, Lambda = 0 dust model with hyperbolic spatial slices; t(a) = C[sqrt(a/C) sqrt(1 + a/C) - arsinh sqrt(a/C)], expanding forever and faster than Einstein-de Sitter.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated as the analogue of Example 18.2 with hyperbolic functions, compared graphically with the flat and closed cases.
concepts.notes: At late times adot tends to 1, i.e. a grows linearly like the empty Milne model (our remark).

concepts.name: Einstein static universe
concepts.definition: The time-independent Robertson-Walker model with dust and a positive cosmological constant Lambda_E: staticity requires k = +1, radius a0 = Lambda_E^-1/2 and dust density rho = Lambda_E/(4 pi).
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated as a way to avoid the 'disturbing' time dependence of all earlier models; Example 18.3 imposes adot = addot = 0 on both Friedmann equations.

concepts.name: critical cosmological constant Lambda_E
concepts.definition: The value of Lambda that exactly balances a given amount of dust in a closed universe, Lambda_E = 4 pi rho at the static radius; for fixed dust constant C it equals 4/(9 C^2).
concepts.how_introduced: Emerges from Example 18.3 and then serves as the reference against which Lemaitre (Lambda > Lambda_E), Eddington-Lemaitre (Lambda = Lambda_E) and Universe 11 (0 < Lambda < Lambda_E) are defined, and as row labels of the grid.
concepts.notes: The formula in terms of C is our derivation from V_eff = C/a + Lambda a^2/3 having minimum value 1.

concepts.name: instability of the Einstein static universe
concepts.definition: Small perturbations of the scale factor about the Einstein static radius obey d^2(delta a)/dt^2 = Lambda_E delta a, so they grow exponentially and the static state is an unstable equilibrium.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 18.4 perturbs the acceleration equation (second minus first Friedmann equation) and closes it with dust conservation; historically credited to Eddington in 1930.
prerequisites: scaling of energy density with the scale factor

concepts.name: linear perturbation analysis
concepts.definition: Writing a quantity as equilibrium value plus a small deviation, keeping first-order terms in the equations of motion, and inspecting whether solutions grow or oscillate.
concepts.how_introduced: Applied to the Einstein universe, following a problem-book approach (Lightman et al.).

concepts.name: effective potential for the scale factor
concepts.definition: Rewriting the first Friedmann equation as adot^2 + 1 = V_eff(a) (for k = 1) so that the universe behaves like a particle with fixed 'energy' moving in a potential; regions with V_eff < 1 are forbidden and the minimum of V_eff marks where expansion is slowest.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced in Example 18.5 to analyse the Lemaitre model with Lambda = (1 + epsilon)^2 Lambda_E, then Taylor-expanded about its minimum in Example 18.6.
concepts.notes: In the book's sign convention V_eff is really minus a potential (it has a minimum where a mechanical potential would have a hilltop); tutors should state this clearly.

concepts.name: Lemaitre universe
concepts.definition: The k = +1 model with dust and Lambda slightly larger than Lambda_E: it emerges from a Big Bang, lingers near the Einstein radius for a long coasting phase, then accelerates into de Sitter-like expansion.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced as a surprise (vacuum energy should give runaway expansion) and analysed with the effective potential; historically identified with Lemaitre's 1931 Primeval Atom proposal.
prerequisites: effective potential for the scale factor

concepts.name: coasting period
concepts.definition: An interval during which a Lemaitre-type universe stays close to a fixed size because its expansion rate is nearly zero; its duration grows like ln(1/epsilon)/sqrt(Lambda) as Lambda approaches Lambda_E from above.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived in Example 18.6 by expanding V_eff quadratically about its minimum, obtaining a sinh solution and asking when the growing term becomes of order one.
prerequisites: effective potential for the scale factor
concepts.notes: The printed prefactor in eqn 18.35 is wrong (should be sqrt(2 epsilon/3)); the logarithmic scaling survives.

concepts.name: Eddington-Lemaitre universe
concepts.definition: The k = +1 model with Lambda exactly Lambda_E that either starts arbitrarily close to the Einstein static state in the infinite past and then expands, or starts from a Big Bang and approaches the static state asymptotically.
concepts.how_introduced: Presented as Eddington's response to the Lemaitre model, avoiding a Big-Bang singularity; shown in both variants distinguished by initial conditions.
prerequisites: instability of the Einstein static universe

concepts.name: bouncing universe
concepts.definition: A k = +1 dust-plus-Lambda model with 0 < Lambda < Lambda_E that, if started at large radius, contracts exponentially, reaches a minimum size and re-expands exponentially; the other branch starting from a Big Bang recollapses to a Big Crunch.
concepts.how_introduced: Offered as the last case in the k = 1 family, with two branches separated by the forbidden region of the effective potential.
prerequisites: effective potential for the scale factor

concepts.name: Hubble's law
concepts.definition: Galaxies recede with speed proportional to distance, v = H0 d, as expected for a homogeneous expanding universe.
concepts.how_introduced: Given historically: established by Hubble in 1929, implicit in Friedmann's 1922 solutions, and noted by Weyl in 1923 for test particles in de Sitter space.

concepts.name: Hubble time as an age bound
concepts.definition: For a universe whose expansion has always decelerated, the tangent to a(t) at the present meets a = 0 at a time 1/H_now before now, which is earlier than the true origin, so the age is less than 1/H_now.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 18.7 with a sketch of a concave a(t) and its extrapolated tangent.
concepts.notes: With acceleration (positive Lambda) the bound can fail.

concepts.name: time-scale problem
concepts.definition: The pre-1950s conflict in which the Hubble-time upper bound on the age of a decelerating universe (about 1.8 billion years) was shorter than the radiometric age of Earth's rocks (at least 3 billion years).
concepts.how_introduced: Framed via Example 18.7; possible fixes discussed are a large Lambda in Lemaitre's model or an Eddington-Lemaitre start from the static state, and the eventual resolution by revised Hubble-constant measurements.
prerequisites: Hubble time as an age bound
concepts.notes: The book also flags a weakness of the Eddington-Lemaitre escape route: it is unclear how stars could condense at the moment expansion begins in a static, homogeneous model.

concepts.name: standard models of cosmology
concepts.definition: The mid-twentieth-century family of Lambda = 0 dust Big-Bang models: Einstein-de Sitter (k = 0), closed (k = 1) and open (k = -1), favoured after the time-scale problem was resolved.
concepts.how_introduced: Named in the history section as the models taken seriously once revised H0 values allowed ages of order 10^10 years without Lambda.
concepts.notes: Superseded since the late 1990s by Lambda-CDM, which has positive Lambda; the term 'standard model' now refers to that.

concepts.name: hot Big Bang
concepts.definition: The picture in which the early universe was extremely hot because temperature scales as 1/a, allowing nuclear fusion of light elements shortly after the singularity.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned as the nuclear-physics support for Big-Bang models promoted by Lemaitre in the 1930s.

concepts.name: cosmic microwave background
concepts.definition: The nearly isotropic black-body radiation filling space, left over from the epoch when the early universe became transparent, now at about 2.73 K with faint anisotropies.
concepts.how_introduced: Presented as the compelling evidence for Big-Bang cosmology: predicted by Alpher and Herman in 1948 (about 5 K), found accidentally by Penzias and Wilson in 1964.

concepts.name: critical density
concepts.definition: The total energy density that makes a Friedmann universe spatially flat for a given Hubble rate, rho_c = 3 H0^2/(8 pi) in G = c = 1 units, i.e. 3 H0^2/(8 pi G) = 1.88e-26 h^2 kg/m^3.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled from Chapter 17 to decide which standard model our Universe resembles, and evaluated numerically.

concepts.name: dimensionless Hubble constant h
concepts.definition: The number h defined by H0 = 100 h km/s/Mpc, used to carry the uncertainty in H0 through formulas; recent values give h close to 0.7.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined when evaluating the critical density, with a margin note and a timeline plot of H0 measurements.

concepts.name: missing mass problem
concepts.definition: The mismatch between the observed density of visible matter (around 1e-28 kg/m^3, far below critical) and evidence that the Universe is spatially flat, implying unseen contributions to the energy density.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated briefly at the end of the history section as an open question.
concepts.notes: Modern resolution: cold dark matter supplies roughly a quarter and dark energy roughly 70 percent of the critical density; the chapter predates this framing and conflates the two.

concepts.name: steady-state theory
concepts.definition: Hoyle's alternative in which continuous matter creation by a negative-energy creation field keeps the density constant as the universe expands, so there is no beginning.
concepts.how_introduced: Described in a margin note on Fred Hoyle, with its abandonment linked to the discovery of the CMB and the story of Hoyle's 1949 BBC coinage of 'Big Bang'.

concepts.name: Milne universe
concepts.definition: The k = -1 Robertson-Walker model with no matter or vacuum energy, a(t) = t, which is flat Minkowski spacetime in hyperbolic slicing.
concepts.how_introduced: Appears only in Exercise 18.1, where a coordinate change reveals the familiar spacetime.

concepts.name: de Sitter hyperboloid
aliases: de Sitter spacetime as an embedded hyperboloid
concepts.definition: De Sitter spacetime realized as the set of points at fixed spacelike 'distance' alpha from the origin of a five-dimensional Minkowski space (one time and four space directions); its induced metric is a vacuum solution with positive Lambda, and toy versions live in 2+1 or 1+1 dimensions.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced in italic linking text inside the exercises, with a hyperboloid figure and embedding calculations.

concepts.name: coordinate slicings of de Sitter spacetime
aliases: closed, flat and open de Sitter slicings
concepts.definition: Different choices of time coordinate on the de Sitter hyperboloid produce Robertson-Walker forms with k = +1 (a = cosh t), k = 0 (a = e^t) or k = -1 (a = sinh t); the flat slicing covers only half of the hyperboloid.
concepts.how_introduced: Exercises 18.6 and 18.7 work this out in 1+1 dimensions, noting that the spatial curvature depends on how spacetime is cut into space and time.
concepts.notes: Exercise 18.6(c) as printed pairs sinh with spherical and cosh with hyperbolic; the Friedmann equation gives the opposite pairing.

concepts.name: static de Sitter coordinates
concepts.definition: A coordinate system on de Sitter space in which the metric is time independent, ds^2 = -(1 - x^2) dt^2 + dx^2/(1 - x^2) in 1+1 dimensions (units alpha = 1), with a horizon at x = 1 and coverage of only part of the hyperboloid.
concepts.how_introduced: Exercise 18.8, noting that a time-independent Lambda makes a static description unsurprising.

key_equations.name: Robertson-Walker line element
key_equations.meaning: Geometry shared by every model in the chapter.
key_equations.symbols: a scale factor; k = -1, 0, +1; r, theta, phi comoving coordinates

key_equations.name: First Friedmann equation (margin)
key_equations.meaning: Expansion rate set by density, curvature and vacuum energy; the equation integrated for each universe.
key_equations.symbols: rho energy density; Lambda cosmological constant; G = c = 1

key_equations.name: Second Friedmann equation (margin)
key_equations.meaning: Space-space Einstein equation; used for staticity and the acceleration equation.

key_equations.name: Hubble parameter and proper-distance growth
key_equations.meaning: Fractional expansion rate; proper separations between comoving observers grow at rate H.

key_equations.name: de Sitter expansion (Universe 1)
key_equations.meaning: Exponential growth with constant H; no singularity.
Flat, Lambda = 0 Friedmann equation; H now depends on time through rho.

key_equations.name: Radiation dilution
key_equations.meaning: Radiation energy density falls as a^-4.
key_equations.symbols: rho_r^(0) radiation density at reference time t0

key_equations.meaning: Friedmann equation for the flat radiation model.
Separable form of the radiation Friedmann equation.

key_equations.name: Radiation-dominated scale factor (Universe 2)
key_equations.meaning: Flat radiation universe grows as t^1/2 from a = 0 at t = 0.
H diverges at t = 0 and decays; hence H0 = 1/(2t0) and rho starts infinite.

key_equations.name: Dust dilution
key_equations.meaning: Pressureless matter density falls as a^-3.
Separable Friedmann equation for flat dust.

key_equations.name: Einstein-de Sitter scale factor (Universe 3)
key_equations.meaning: Flat dust universe grows as t^2/3.

key_equations.name: Dust-plus-vacuum Friedmann equation
key_equations.meaning: Master equation for all dust-and-Lambda models of any curvature; basis of the summary grid.
Flat case of 18.11: dust term dominates at small a, Lambda term at large a.

key_equations.name: Flat dust plus Lambda solution (Universe 4)
key_equations.meaning: Interpolates between t^2/3 growth and exponential expansion; equivalently a proportional to sinh^(2/3)(sqrt(3 Lambda) t/2). Verified numerically.

key_equations.name: Turnaround radius for negative Lambda
key_equations.meaning: Where adot vanishes in the flat Lambda < 0 dust model; expansion must stop there.

key_equations.name: Flat dust with negative Lambda (Universe 5)
key_equations.meaning: Big Bang, maximum radius, Big Crunch. Verified numerically.
Lambda = 0 dust models of any curvature.
Closed dust equation after substitution.
Integral form with Big-Bang initial condition u(0) = 0.
Standard integral.

key_equations.name: Closed dust universe (Universe 6)
key_equations.meaning: Time as a function of radius: rises to a = C then recollapses (a cycloid). Verified by differentiation.

key_equations.name: Open dust universe (Universe 7)
key_equations.meaning: Unbounded expansion, faster than Einstein-de Sitter. Verified by differentiation.
First Friedmann equation for dust plus Lambda_E.
Staticity imposed on the first equation.
Second equation at rest (p = 0): forces k = +1.

key_equations.name: Einstein static universe parameters
key_equations.latex: a_0=\Lambda_{\rm E}^{-1/2},\qquad \rho_{\rm d}^{(0)}=\frac{\Lambda_{\rm E}}{4\pi},\qquad a_0=(4\pi\rho_{\rm d}^{(0)})^{-1/2}
key_equations.meaning: Radius and dust density of the balanced closed universe.

key_equations.name: Acceleration equation for dust plus Lambda_E
key_equations.meaning: Second minus first Friedmann equation: matter decelerates, Lambda accelerates.
Linearized acceleration equation.
Conservation of dust.
Density perturbation tied to radius perturbation.

key_equations.name: Einstein-universe instability
key_equations.latex: \ddot{\delta a}=\Lambda_{\rm E}\,\delta a,\qquad \delta a\propto e^{\sqrt{\Lambda_{\rm E}}\,t}
key_equations.meaning: Perturbation grows exponentially: unstable equilibrium. (The reading-copy OCR places t inside the square root; the printed page has sqrt(Lambda_E) times t.)
Dust density expressed in Einstein-universe units.
k = 1 Friedmann equation as an energy equation.

key_equations.name: Effective potential (Lemaitre model)
key_equations.meaning: Dust term falls as 1/a, vacuum term grows as a^2; minimum controls coasting.
key_equations.symbols: epsilon small positive excess of Lambda over Lambda_E

key_equations.name: Radius of slowest expansion
key_equations.meaning: Location of the minimum of V_eff, i.e. minimum of adot (not of a). Verified.
Quadratic expansion about a_min using V(a_min) = (1+epsilon)^(2/3) and V'' = 2 Lambda. Verified.
Solution near the coasting radius; t_m is the time of minimum adot. Consistent with 18.33.

key_equations.name: Small-epsilon coasting solution (printed prefactor incorrect)
key_equations.meaning: Expanding [1-(1+epsilon)^(-2/3)]^(1/2) gives sqrt(2 epsilon/3), not epsilon/3 as printed; we give the corrected form.
Condition for the end of coasting as printed; with the corrected prefactor it should read sqrt(2 epsilon/3) sinh(...) ~ 1.

key_equations.name: Coasting duration
key_equations.meaning: Coasting lasts a time logarithmic in 1/epsilon. With the corrected prefactor the one-sided time is about ln(1/epsilon)/(2 Lambda^1/2); the full plateau on both sides of t_m is about ln(1/epsilon)/Lambda^1/2, which our numerical integration confirms.

key_equations.name: Universe 11 asymptotics
key_equations.meaning: Bouncing branch: exponential contraction then exponential re-expansion.
Tangent line at t_now reaches a = 0 at t_1.

key_equations.name: Hubble-time age bound
key_equations.latex: t_{\rm now}-t_1=\frac{a(t_{\rm now})}{\dot a(t_{\rm now})}=H(t_{\rm now})^{-1}
key_equations.meaning: For always-decelerating expansion the age T is less than 1/H_now.

key_equations.name: Temperature scaling
key_equations.meaning: Early universe hot enough for nucleosynthesis.

key_equations.name: Critical density
key_equations.meaning: Density that makes the universe flat; numerical value restores G (checked: 3H^2/8 pi G for h = 1 is 1.878e-26 kg/m^3).

key_equations.name: Milne universe line element (Ex. 18.1)
key_equations.meaning: Empty k = -1 model; with r = t sinh chi, T = t cosh chi (18.41) it becomes Minkowski space.

key_equations.name: Milne-to-Minkowski transformation (Ex. 18.1)
key_equations.meaning: Maps the empty open universe onto the interior of the future light cone of Minkowski space.

key_equations.name: de Sitter hyperboloid
key_equations.meaning: Embedding of de Sitter spacetime in 4+1 Minkowski space.

key_equations.name: Intermediate line element on the 2+1 hyperboloid (Ex. 18.6a)
key_equations.meaning: Induced metric after eliminating Y, in variables v and psi; a further substitution v = sinh chi gives eqn 18.44.

key_equations.name: Open slicing of 1+1 de Sitter (Ex. 18.6)
key_equations.meaning: Friedmann form with a = sinh; corresponds to k = -1 (book text says spherical, which is swapped).

key_equations.name: Closed slicing of 1+1 de Sitter
key_equations.meaning: Friedmann form with a = cosh; corresponds to k = +1.

key_equations.name: Hyperboloid metric with Y eliminated (Ex. 18.7)
key_equations.meaning: Induced metric on -T^2 + X^2 + Y^2 = 1 written in T and X, using Y dY = T dT - X dX.

key_equations.name: Flat-slicing coordinates on the hyperboloid
key_equations.meaning: Satisfy -T^2 + X^2 + Y^2 = 1 identically; since T + X = e^t > 0 they cover only the half of the hyperboloid with X > -T.

key_equations.name: Flat slicing of 1+1 de Sitter (Ex. 18.7)
key_equations.meaning: Universe 1 in 1+1 dimensions, covering half the hyperboloid.

key_equations.name: Conformally flat (Poincaré) form
key_equations.meaning: Flat-slicing de Sitter rewritten in conformal time.

key_equations.name: Static-patch coordinates (corrected)
key_equations.meaning: Book prints (1-x)^(1/2) in the T equation; (1-x^2)^(1/2) is required for 18.51 (checked numerically).

key_equations.name: Static de Sitter line element
key_equations.meaning: Time-independent, Schwarzschild-like form with horizon at x = 1.

figures.label: Fig. 18.1
figures.caption_paraphrase: History of the flat, Lambda = 0 radiation and dust universes: flat 3-spaces growing without limit from a Big-Bang point.
figures.visual_description: A 3D perspective sketch of a parabolic bowl whose lowest point is a single vertex. Four horizontal square grids (about 5 by 5 cells) are stacked up the bowl; the bottom one is small and the grids get progressively larger toward the open top, the largest forming a lid. An arrow labelled 'time' points upward at the right.
figures.what_it_teaches: Flat spatial sections of a k = 0 universe keep their Euclidean geometry while the scale factor grows from zero; the vertex is the Big Bang.

redesign.idea: Stacked flat grids whose cell size follows a(t) for radiation or dust, with comoving galaxy dots fixed to grid nodes and a live clock.
redesign.interaction: Learner toggles radiation versus dust and scrubs time; the grid spacing, the outline of the bowl and a small a(t) inset update, and a warning explains that the apex point is a cartoon because flat space is infinite at all times.

figures.label: Fig. 18.2
figures.caption_paraphrase: Comparison of a(t) for the flat de Sitter, radiation and Einstein-de Sitter models.
figures.visual_description: Axes a(t) (vertical) and t (horizontal) with a tick at t0. Three curves meet at a common point above t0. The exponential, labelled e^{H0(t-t0)}, starts at a positive intercept on the a-axis, runs below the power laws until t0 and then rises steeply above them. The curves labelled t^{2/3} and t^{1/2} both start at the origin; t^{1/2} lies above t^{2/3} before t0 and below it afterwards.
figures.what_it_teaches: Only the vacuum model avoids a = 0; the power laws differ in how fast they rise from the singularity and how they decelerate.

redesign.idea: Normalized a(t) explorer for the three flat models with a companion H(t) panel.
redesign.interaction: Learner drags t0 (the matching time) and switches between linear and log-log axes; power laws become straight lines of slope 1/2 and 2/3, the exponential curves away, and H(t) = 1/(2t), 2/(3t) or constant is plotted below.

figures.caption_paraphrase: Table comparing the three flat models by composition, a(t), H(t) and whether they have a Big Bang.
figures.visual_description: A three-column typeset table (de Sitter, Radiation, Einstein-de Sitter) with rows Composition (energy, radiation, dust), a(t) (a0 e^{H0(t-t0)}, a0(2H0 t)^{1/2}, a0(3H0 t/2)^{2/3}), H(t) (const., 1/(2t), 2/(3t)) and Big Bang (No, Yes, Yes). No image was exported; description from the rendered page 207.
figures.what_it_teaches: Condenses the flat-model results into a comparison that shows the link between composition, power-law index and singularity.

redesign.idea: Equation-of-state slider card: a single parameter w (p = w rho) generates the table row a proportional to t^{2/(3(1+w))} and H = 2/(3(1+w)t).
redesign.interaction: Learner slides w from -1 to 1/3; the card shows the density scaling, a(t), H(t) and Big-Bang yes/no, snapping to the three tabulated cases.

figures.label: Fig. 18.3
figures.caption_paraphrase: History of flat Universe 5 with negative vacuum energy: expansion followed by recollapse.
figures.visual_description: A tall spindle or lens shaped outline drawn in perspective, closed to a point at both top and bottom. Four horizontal square grids sit inside; they are small near the ends and largest in the middle. A slanted arrow labelled 'time' points upward at lower right.
figures.what_it_teaches: Even flat space can recollapse if the vacuum energy is negative: size rises from a Big Bang to a maximum and returns to a Big Crunch.

redesign.idea: Animated flat grid breathing out and in, driven by eqn 18.14, with the turnaround radius marked.
redesign.interaction: Learner sets C and |Lambda|; the animation length, the maximum grid size (a_max^3 = 3C/|Lambda|) and a synchronized a(t) curve update.

figures.label: Fig. 18.4(a)
figures.caption_paraphrase: Radius function of the closed (k = 1) Lambda = 0 dust model, Universe 6.
figures.visual_description: Panel (a) with axes a(t) and t, labelled 'Lambda = 0, k = 1'. A single low, symmetric arch starts at the origin, rises to a rounded maximum and returns to the t-axis.
figures.what_it_teaches: Closed dust universe begins and ends with singularities.

redesign.idea: Rolling-wheel animation that traces the cycloid a = (C/2)(1 - cos eta), t = (C/2)(eta - sin eta) equivalent to eqn 18.19.
redesign.interaction: Learner adjusts the dust constant C (wheel diameter); the arch height C and lifetime pi C scale accordingly, and a marker shows the moment of maximum expansion.

figures.label: Fig. 18.4(b)
figures.caption_paraphrase: Radius function of the flat Einstein-de Sitter model for comparison.
figures.visual_description: Panel (b) with axes a(t) and t labelled 'E-dS' and 'Lambda = 0, k = 0'. A concave curve rises from the origin, steep at first and steadily flattening, with no maximum.
figures.what_it_teaches: The flat dust model sits on the boundary between recollapse and eternal expansion.

redesign.idea: Overlay of the three Lambda = 0 dust models on common axes with a draggable density parameter.
redesign.interaction: Learner drags Omega_matter through 1; the curve morphs continuously between the open, flat and closed shapes and labels the fate.

figures.label: Fig. 18.4(c)
figures.caption_paraphrase: Radius function of the open (k = -1) Lambda = 0 dust model, Universe 7.
figures.visual_description: Panel (c) with axes a(t) and t labelled 'Lambda = 0, k = -1'. A curve rises from the origin with initial steepness and then becomes nearly a straight line of constant slope, ending higher than the E-dS curve of panel (b).
figures.what_it_teaches: Open dust universes expand forever, approaching constant adot (coasting like an empty universe) at late times.

redesign.idea: Same overlay as panel (b), with an asymptote line adot = 1 drawn for the open case.
redesign.interaction: Learner scrubs time to see the open curve approach its linear asymptote while the flat curve keeps bending over.

figures.label: Fig. 18.5
figures.caption_paraphrase: History of Universe 6: 3-spheres (drawn as circles) that grow and shrink.
figures.visual_description: A closed, rounded barrel or lemon shaped surface drawn freehand, with dots marking a point at the bottom and at the top. Horizontal ellipses (solid in front, dashed behind) cut the surface; the middle ellipse is widest and bold. A curved arrow labelled 'time' runs up the lower right side.
figures.what_it_teaches: Each time slice of a closed universe is a finite 3-sphere; its radius follows the cycloid from Big Bang to Big Crunch.

redesign.idea: A 2-sphere stand-in for the 3-sphere inflating and deflating, with comoving galaxies and a light ray circling it.
redesign.interaction: Learner scrubs cosmic time; the sphere radius follows eqn 18.19, galaxy separations scale, and a photon launched at the Big Bang shows how far round the sphere it gets before the crunch.

figures.label: Fig. 18.6
figures.caption_paraphrase: History of Universe 7: hyperbolic 3-spaces expanding without limit.
figures.visual_description: A funnel or cone shaped surface opening upward from a single point at the bottom, drawn freehand. Horizontal ellipses of increasing size (dashed at the back, a small dotted one near the tip) mark slices; a straight arrow labelled 'time' points diagonally up at the lower right.
figures.what_it_teaches: Open universe slices are infinite hyperbolic spaces (only schematically represented) that expand forever from a Big Bang.

redesign.idea: Poincaré-disk view of a hyperbolic slice whose geodesic triangles and galaxy spacing scale with a(t).
redesign.interaction: Learner scrubs time and drags a triangle; its physical area grows with a^2 while its angle deficit shrinks, showing curvature radius a(t).

figures.label: Fig. 18.7
figures.caption_paraphrase: Universe 8, the Einstein static universe, as a stack of equal 3-spheres.
figures.visual_description: A vertical cylinder with hatched edges, crossed by about six equal horizontal ellipses (front solid, back dashed). An upward arrow labelled 'time' stands to the right.
figures.what_it_teaches: A static closed universe has constant radius for all time, balanced by Lambda_E.

redesign.idea: Balanced cylinder with a 'nudge' button that adds or removes a tiny amount of dust.
redesign.interaction: Learner nudges the density; the cylinder begins to flare out (de Sitter-like) or pinch in (collapse) at a rate set by exp(sqrt(Lambda_E) t), and a side plot shows delta a versus time on log axes.

figures.label: Fig. 18.8
figures.caption_paraphrase: Universe 9 (Lemaitre): Big Bang, a long near-static stretch, then renewed expansion.
figures.visual_description: A vase or trumpet shaped surface: a point at the bottom, a rapidly widening base, a nearly cylindrical middle section crossed by several ellipses, and a strongly flared rim at the top. A curved arrow labelled 'time' runs up the right side.
figures.what_it_teaches: The coasting phase appears as the straight-sided waist; afterwards Lambda takes over.

redesign.idea: Shape-of-history generator: the surface of revolution is drawn live from numerically integrated a(t).
redesign.interaction: Learner lowers epsilon on a log slider; the cylindrical waist lengthens by equal steps for each factor of ten, illustrating ln(1/epsilon) scaling.

figures.label: Fig. 18.9(a)
figures.caption_paraphrase: Radius function of Universe 9 (L) with its coasting plateau.
figures.visual_description: Panel (a), axes a(t) and t, label 'L' and 'Lambda > Lambda_E, k = 1'. The curve shoots up from the origin, bends into a broad nearly flat plateau, then curves upward again (inflection in the middle).
figures.what_it_teaches: Loitering: slow expansion near the Einstein radius separates the dust-dominated and vacuum-dominated eras.

redesign.idea: Two linked panels: the effective potential V_eff(a) with a horizontal 'energy' line at 1 and a bead, and the a(t) curve.
redesign.interaction: Learner changes epsilon; the potential's minimum sinks just below the line, the bead slows as it crosses the dip, and the plateau in a(t) grows.

figures.label: Fig. 18.9(b)
figures.caption_paraphrase: Universe 8 (E) and the two forms of Universe 10 (E-L), with Lambda = Lambda_E.
figures.visual_description: Panel (b), axes a(t) and t, labels 'E-L', 'E' and 'Lambda = Lambda_E, k = 1'. A horizontal line at constant a (short dashed portion at left) is labelled E. One curve starts just on the line at early times and later rises steeply (E-L); another starts at the origin and rises to approach the line from below asymptotically.
figures.what_it_teaches: At exactly Lambda_E the static state is a separatrix: models can peel off it into expansion or creep up to it from a Big Bang.

redesign.idea: Phase portrait in the (a, adot) plane showing the separatrix through the Einstein point.
redesign.interaction: Learner clicks initial conditions; trajectories are integrated and colour-coded (collapse, asymptotic static, runaway), and the two E-L branches appear as the separatrix arms.

figures.label: Fig. 18.9(c)
figures.caption_paraphrase: Two branches of Universe 11 with 0 < Lambda < Lambda_E.
figures.visual_description: Panel (c), axes a(t) and t, label '0 < Lambda < Lambda_E, k = 1'. An upper curve starts high at t = 0, falls to a minimum and rises again (a bounce); a lower curve is an arch starting and ending on the t-axis.
figures.what_it_teaches: Below Lambda_E a forbidden band of radii separates a recollapsing Big-Bang branch from a singularity-free bounce.
concepts: effective potential for the scale factor

redesign.idea: Effective potential with the energy line cutting it in two places, highlighting the forbidden band.
redesign.interaction: Learner lowers Lambda below Lambda_E; the forbidden band opens, and clicking on either side launches the arch or the bounce solution.

figures.label: Fig. 18.10
figures.caption_paraphrase: Grid of origins and fates of dust-plus-Lambda Robertson-Walker models, computed from eqn 18.11.
figures.visual_description: A full-page 5-row by 3-column grid of small a-versus-t plots. Columns are headed k = -1, k = 0, k = 1; rows are labelled Lambda > Lambda_E, Lambda = Lambda_E, 0 < Lambda < Lambda_E, Lambda = 0, Lambda < 0. Bold labels mark U9 (top right, plateau curve), U8, U10 (second row right: horizontal line plus a rising and an asymptotically approaching curve), U11 (third row right: a bounce curve above an arch), U7, U3, U6 (Lambda = 0 row: open, flat, arch). In the first three rows the k = -1 and k = 0 panels show ever-rising curves, bending upward more for larger Lambda; the bottom row shows recollapsing arches in all three columns.
figures.what_it_teaches: The whole chapter as a lookup table: for Lambda <= 0 geometry and sign of Lambda fix fate; for positive Lambda only the closed column shows static, loitering and bouncing behaviour.

redesign.idea: Continuous (Omega_m, Omega_Lambda) or (k, Lambda) explorer replacing the discrete grid, with regions coloured by origin and fate.
redesign.interaction: Learner drags a point across the plane; a(t) is integrated from eqn 18.11 in real time, and boundary curves (Lambda = Lambda_E = 4/(9C^2) for k = 1, Lambda = 0) highlight where behaviour changes; clicking a boundary snaps to the book's numbered universes.

figures.label: Fig. 18.11
figures.caption_paraphrase: Universe 10 (Eddington-Lemaitre) sits near the Einstein state and then expands.
figures.visual_description: A vertical cylinder crossed by equal ellipses in its lower part, widening into a flared, trumpet-like mouth at the top. Several small upward arrows and a 'time' label run up the right side.
figures.what_it_teaches: A universe with no Big Bang that has existed near the static radius indefinitely before expanding.

redesign.idea: Surface-of-revolution history generated from the separatrix solution, with a movable 'departure time'.
redesign.interaction: Learner drags the tiny initial displacement from the static state; the length of the cylinder section changes logarithmically.

figures.label: Fig. 18.12

A dashed straight line tangent at the dot extends back to hit the t-axis at t_1, to the left of the curve's start. A double-headed arrow below the axis marks T from the curve's start to t_now.
